plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately determining thermal properties of quantum systems while maintaining a fixed particle count. Researchers devised a simulation method combining state preparation, Trotterization, and quantum signal processing to estimate key thermodynamic quantities. The approach allows for flexible adjustment of chemical potential through classical post-processing, reducing the need for repeated quantum computations, and demonstrates improved computational efficiency compared to classical alternatives for specific Hamiltonian models.

fulltext.summary: The work introduces a quantum signal processing framework for estimating thermal properties of Hamiltonians while preserving particle number. The approach utilizes mixed Dicke states, Trotterized simulation, and Algorithm 1 for canonical calculations, followed by Algorithm 2 for grand-canonical reconstruction via classical reweighting of measurement data. Numerical validation was performed on the two-dimensional Hubbard model, demonstrating that the proposed methods can outperform classical Lanczos methods up to polynomial factors, with specific parameter settings like a Krylov subspace dimension of 40 and 30 Rademacher vectors.

items.title: A Scoping Review and Experimental Study on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for Human-Robot Collaboration
items.abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) can facilitate mass customisation in Industry 4.0, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) representing a promising approach for developing safe AI-based robots. Practical challenges remain regarding safety during AI development, human feedback quality, and bidirectional human-robot adaptation. We conducted a scoping review of RLHF in HRC systems, mapping methods that address these challenges. Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 199 records and included 20 peer-reviewed publications (2020-2025) spanning multiple HRC domains. To our knowledge, this is the first review focused on the bidirectional, closed-loop design of RLHF. Our review found multiple feedback modalities enabling data collection in various feedback formats. Collected data can be integrated at different stages of AI training, resulting in a multi-step development process. Pilot experiments are commonly used to evaluate HRC systems based on both human and robot metrics. To empirically test a key gap identified in the review, we conducted a between-subjects VR experiment comparing system- and user-initiated feedback on robot proxemic behaviour for safe navigation. Using Bayesian models, we analysed the relation between the collected feedback and safety metrics: psychological safety (post-experiment questionnaire) and physical safety (inverse time-to-collision). Results show that user-initiated feedback captures perceived safety better than system-initiated feedback, indicating that feedback timing directly affects feedback quality. Our review and experiment findings show that RLHF relies on appropriate feedback methods to ensure AI safety in HRC, and future RLHF research should prioritise realistic HRC experiments evaluating the effects of feedback collection methods on relevant human and robot metrics.
excerpts: [2.3 Results] Developing RLHF algorithms for HRC generally requires a multi-step process to achieve the desired AI-based robot learning performance (see Figure 4). Using pre-training for the RL task before collecting human feedback [ 24, 39, 44, 45, 46 ] ensures a functioning initial policy that can then be fine-tuned and customised according to user input through subsequent learning sessions. RL algorithms can be pre-trained using trial-and-error approaches in simulation, allowing the robot to learn independently, or by incorporating synthetic human feedback to introduce human evaluation early in the learning process [ 20, 31, 30, 45 ]. These methods enable training on a large quantity of trials and data that would otherwise be difficult, if not impossible, to collect through real interaction with the environment and users. For modelling both the synthetic and the real human feedback, Bayesian methods can be employed to create distributions of the human data and account for feedback uncertainty [ 31, 46, 49 ]. Caption: Figure 4: RLHF development methodology for robotic applications with iterative training stages

[2.3 Results] Experiments for collecting human feedback can be set up in various environments that provide different levels of realism. On the one hand, 2D or 3D computer simulations offer an easy-to-use framework for displaying AI-based robot behaviour and collecting human feedback [ 20, 31, 30, 38, 47, 23 ]. On the other hand, realistic (mock-up) environments require more space and functional physical assets [ 23, 32, 44, 45, 47 ], but offer greater realism and the opportunity to collect more representative feedback data. Additionally, an important consideration for meaningful experiments in realistic environments is the participant count and background. Pilot studies are carried out with a relatively small number of participants ( $<25$) [ 20, 24, 25, 29, 32, 42, 44, 45, 46, 49 ], while fewer large-scale studies exist [ 31, 30, 38, 39, 47 ]. Furthermore, although these large-scale studies include more participants, they are not representative of the intended target groups.

[2.3 Results] The human-to-robot direction within HTL concerns the effects on the AI-based robot and collaboration outcomes (see Figure 5). Within the context of RLHF for HRC applications, AI-based robot performance can be evaluated on two levels. Firstly, AI learning properties determine the suitability of the RL model for the intended task and target users. AI learning can be quantified using quality metrics such as learning efficiency [ 17, 20, 23, 30, 31, 44, 45 ], often assessed alongside adaptability [ 39, 32, 2, 24, 25 ], or explainability (especially in terms of predictability) [ 16 ]. These metrics represent AI characteristics necessary for enabling the robot to perform highly flexible tasks. Secondly, the robot’s resulting behaviour directly impacts overall HRC system outcomes. While most studies focus only on robot task performance metrics (e.g., efficiency in task execution) [ 16, 25, 31, 42, 46, 47, 49 ], others specifically focus on robot actions that impact system safety (e.g., collisions in navigation) [ 2, 44, 17, 20 ]. Caption: Figure 5: HRC safety and performance for the closed-loop RLHF design: AI-based robot, human and feedback metrics

[2.4 Discussion] RLHF research for HRC can benefit from focusing solutions on target applications. When it comes to feedback formats and collection methods, tailored solutions should be developed for specific use cases [ 27, 28 ]. For example, an industrial environment with specific HRC tasks might impose various constraints on the RLHF methodology, such as environment sound and light conditions, monitoring capabilities, available interaction modalities, time and cognitive limitations, procedural standards, resource availability. These constraints limit the viability of different feedback methods and should be considered early in the design and development of RLHF strategies. Therefore, future research should attempt to integrate and test in realistic set-ups with target user groups.

plain.summary: This study investigates the application of a specific machine learning paradigm within the context of human-robot interaction. Researchers undertook a systematic review of existing literature and a novel experiment to examine the impact of feedback timing on safety perceptions and physical safety during robot navigation. The investigation employed virtual reality to compare user-initiated versus system-initiated feedback, revealing that user-initiated feedback more accurately reflects perceived safety. The findings highlight the importance of feedback methodology in ensuring the safety and efficacy of AI-driven robotic systems.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates the application of reinforcement learning techniques incorporating human feedback within the context of human-robot collaboration. A scoping review of 20 peer-reviewed publications (2020-2025) was conducted, identifying common feedback modalities and integration strategies within a multi-step development process. To empirically test a gap identified in the review, a VR experiment compared system- and user-initiated feedback on robot proxemic behavior, revealing that user-initiated feedback better captured perceived safety, as measured by a post-experiment questionnaire and inverse time-to-collision. The study highlights the importance of feedback timing and the need for realistic HRC experiments evaluating the effects of feedback collection methods.

items.title: A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites
items.abstract: Modeling heterogeneous materials remains a challenge for physics-informed neural networks such as the deep energy method (DEM). The DEM and its variants, here collectively referred to as the neural energy method (NEM), offer a differentiable variational framework. However, their conventional collocation-based implementation (C-NEM) often suffers from physically inadmissible displacement oscillations, integration errors, and high computational costs from automatic differentiation. This work introduces the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization of the displacement field. By interpolating nodal displacements via shape functions, the M-NEM imposes a kinematic constraint that suppresses oscillations. Furthermore, the method replaces automatic differentiation with algebraic shape function derivatives for strain computation and employs high-order Gaussian quadrature for accurate energy integration. On a directly comparable benchmark problem, the M-NEM reduces stress errors by up to three orders of magnitude relative to the C-NEM while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. On two further benchmarks involving extreme stiffness contrasts, only the M-NEM converges. A comparative study of neural architectures reveals that radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) yield optimal performance within the M-NEM, resolving sharp gradients at material interfaces with higher accuracy than multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with random Fourier feature (RFF) mapping and faster convergence than Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs).
excerpts: [1 Introduction] To address these issues, the current work proposes the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization. Shape-function interpolation, algebraic derivatives, and element-level Gaussian quadrature address the first three challenges. The fourth challenge of spectral bias is addressed by investigating the efficacy of alternative network architectures within this framework in a comparative study of MLPs with RFF mapping, KANs, and RBFNNs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the continuum mechanics foundation, the general NEM formulation, and the examined neural network architectures. Section 3 presents the methodology of the M-NEM and details how mesh-based discretization benefits the training process. Section 4 validates the approach through benchmark problems involving stiff inclusions and real-world material composites. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the findings and discusses future directions.

[2.2 Network implementation and optimization] In the conventional implementation, referred to in the current work as the C-NEM, the energy functional is evaluated on a set of collocation points and the deformation gradient is computed via automatic differentiation. This introduces three limitations that become critical for the simulation of heterogeneous composites. A sufficiently expressive network may produce physically inadmissible displacement oscillations between collocation points that remain invisible to the loss function as they do not affect the energy evaluated at the sampling locations, a phenomenon here referred to as geometric overfitting. Furthermore, computing the deformation gradient via automatic differentiation grows the computational graph with network depth and the number of integration points, increasing memory consumption and sensitivity to floating point precision. Finally, stochastic or low-order integration schemes introduce aliasing errors when the strain energy density varies abruptly across material interfaces.

[4.5 Carbon fiber reinforced polymer] The quantitative performance is compared in Fig. 12. The stress error analysis confirms the qualitative observations, with the RBFNN outperforming the KAN by almost two orders of magnitude. Notably, the runtime analysis demonstrates the computational efficiency of the RBFNN architecture, which achieves a high-fidelity solution more than ten times faster than the KAN. This performance gap stems from the architectural nature of the models. The multi-layer composition of deep neural networks leads to a non-convex optimization landscape, whereas the fixed-center RBFNN yields a displacement field that is linear with respect to the trainable weights. plain.summary: The study addresses limitations in existing neural energy methods for simulating complex material structures. Researchers developed a mesh-based approach, termed M-NEM, to improve the stability and efficiency of these methods by incorporating shape functions for displacement interpolation and algebraic derivatives for strain calculation. Results demonstrate significant reductions in stress errors and computational time compared to conventional methods, alongside improved convergence for problems with extreme material property variations. The investigation also identifies radial basis function neural networks as a superior architecture for accurately representing material interfaces.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces a mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM) to address limitations in conventional neural energy methods (NEM) when simulating heterogeneous materials. The M-NEM utilizes shape functions to interpolate nodal displacements, enabling kinematic constraints that suppress oscillations and replacing automatic differentiation with algebraic derivatives for strain computation. The method was validated on benchmark problems involving stiff inclusions and real-world composites, demonstrating a reduction in stress errors by up to three orders of magnitude compared to the conventional collocation-based NEM (C-NEM) and a speedup of one to two orders of magnitude, with radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) proving optimal for resolving sharp gradients. The study compared RBFNNs to multi-layer perceptrons with random Fourier feature mapping and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, finding RBFNNs to be ten times faster and exhibiting significantly lower stress error.

items.title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
items.abstract: Multi-domain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) flexibly model medium-specific representations to solve fluid--solid conjugate heat transfer (CHT). However, standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports, which can yield plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures. We propose Cova-PINN, a multi-domain PINN framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. Cova-PINN jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. We evaluate Cova-PINN on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a geometrically distinct DualMS design against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol. Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors across the four TPMS topologies by $37.7\%$ and $60.2\%$, respectively, while also improving full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS.

Stage 2 updates only the thermal parameters $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ and retains the standard energy equations, boundary conditions, and interface transmission in the Pointwise block. On this basis, Cova-PINN performs global–local conservation co-optimization: Local couples the temperature networks through shared finite-region balances along the thermal interaction path, while Global closes the accumulated heat transfer at the exchanger scale. plain.summary: This work addresses the challenge of accurately modeling heat transfer across multiple physical domains, specifically in complex geometries. The researchers developed a novel physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework, termed Cova-PINN, which focuses on aligning conservation principles and thermal interactions at both local and global scales. Through comparative testing on several heat exchanger designs, the proposed method demonstrated significant improvements in outlet temperature accuracy and overall energy transfer compared to existing PINN approaches. The study highlights the importance of cross-domain conservation in achieving reliable simulations.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses challenges in solving fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer problems using physics-informed neural networks. A new framework, Cova-PINN, is proposed to improve energy transfer accuracy by aligning conservation supports with thermal interaction paths and jointly optimizing local and global balances. The method was evaluated on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a DualMS design, demonstrating a 37.7% reduction in average outlet-temperature error and a 60.2% reduction in device-level closure error compared to the MUSA-PINN-CHT baseline. The simulations were performed at a Reynolds number of 100 with inlet temperatures of 80°C and 20°C, using ANSYS CFX as a reference.

items.abstract: In this paper, we establish a quantitative finite-time approximation of scattering fields for nonlinear Alfvén waves in three-dimensional ideal incompressible magnetohydrodynamics near a strong constant magnetic background. Using the global weighted estimates, we prove that truncating the scattering profiles at time $T$ introduces an error in both the $L^\infty$ norm and the $H^{N_*+1}$ norm of order $$ O\bigl(\varepsilon^2(R+T)^{-δ}\bigr), $$ where $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ measures the size of the initial perturbation, $R\ge100$ is the scale parameter in the weighted energy, $δ\in(0,2/3)$ is the exponent related to weights, and $N_*+1$ is the Sobolev regularity order assumed for the initial data. The pointwise estimate follows from the decay of the nonlocal pressure along nonlinear characteristics, while the Sobolev estimate combines higher-order weighted pressure bounds with estimates for derivatives of the characteristic flows. Numerical experiments measure pointwise and Sobolev pressure-integral tails to verify the quadratic dependence of the initial perturbation amplitude.

A finite-time truncation method is developed, and error bounds are derived in both norm and Sobolev space, dependent on parameters related to the initial perturbation and the scale of the problem. The study validates these theoretical bounds through numerical simulations that examine the behavior of pressure fields.

fulltext.summary: The study investigates the approximation of scattering fields for Alfvén waves in a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic system. A finite-time approximation is developed, demonstrating an error bound of order $$ O\bigl(\varepsilon^2(R+T)^{-δ}\bigr) $$ in both the $L^\infty$ norm and the $H^{N_*+1}$ norm. Numerical validation using a Fourier pseudospectral method with a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme and Helmholtz–Leray projection confirms the quadratic dependence of the initial perturbation amplitude on the unweighted $H^{6}$ tail error.

items.title: A posteriori error estimation for coarse or distorted meshes
items.abstract: Finite element simulations carried out on meshes issued from real-world geometries - patient-specific anatomies, scanned industrial parts, fractured media - almost never satisfy the shape-regularity assumptions under which classical a posteriori error analysis is written. Practitioners are therefore left without a quantitative answer to a very legitimate question: how wrong is my simulation when my mesh is coarse and contains badly shaped elements? In this work, we study to which extent equilibrated flux estimators can provide such an answer. Indeed, they deliver a guaranteed and fully computable upper bound of the energy-norm discretization error, with a constant equal to one; and, crucially for the present study, its derivation uses no shape-regularity, quasi-uniformity or angle condition. The only geometric ingredient is the Poincaré constant on a single cell, which Payne and Weinberger showed to be at most hK /pi on any convex cell K, however distorted (hK being the cell size). Mesh quality affects the local efficiency - the sharpness of the estimator - but never its reliability, so that the failure mode under distortion is pessimism rather than false confidence.
excerpts: [1.1 Contributions and outline] We restrict ourselves to the Poisson problem with a piecewise constant coefficient, to conforming Lagrange elements, and — in the experiments — to two space dimensions and low order piecewise linear finite element approximation. These choices are motivated by the following. The phenomenon we want to isolate is geometric, and every additional feature of the model would make it harder to attribute an effect to the mesh alone. The consequences of relaxing each of these restrictions are discussed in Section 11. We also do not address the algebraic error: all linear systems below are solved by a direct method.

[10 Numerical experiments] All computations are performed with FEniCSx ( dolfinx 0.9.0) in serial. All the scripts, meshes and raw result files are openly available at https://github.com/michelduprez/A-posteriori-error-estimation-for-coarse-or-distorted-meshes Every table and figure below is regenerated from that repository by a single driver, whose README documents the role of each file. Related open implementations are dolfin-tape [ 10 ] and the Bank–Weiser code of [ 17 ].

[10.1 Protocol] locally damaged meshes: one single interior vertex is displaced, all other cells being left untouched, in the spirit of [ 29 ]. Two variants, controlled by a parameter $t\in\{10^{-1},\dots,10^{-4}\}$: needle, where the vertex is moved a fraction $1-t$ of the way toward a neighbour (so $\theta_{\min}\to 0$ while $\theta_{\max}$ stays bounded away from $\pi$, and the maximum angle condition still holds); and cap, where it is moved onto the opposite edge of one of its cells (so $\theta_{\max}\to\pi$ and the maximum angle condition fails). In both cases $s_{K}\sim t$; extent of the damage: $m\in\{1,4,16,64\}$ vertices are cap-damaged at fixed $t=10^{-3}$, either scattered over the whole domain or grouped in a single contiguous block. At equal $m$ and equal local quality, the two layouts differ only by the diameter of the damaged region, which is precisely the parameter the conjecture of Section 7.3 points to. Damaged vertices are taken on the even sublattice so that no two of them are neighbours; globally anisotropic structured meshes with $N\times M$ cells, $M\in\{N,N/4,N/8,N/16\}$, hence aspect ratios up to $\alpha\approx 16$;

[10.10 Bank–Weiser: sharper on good meshes, more fragile on bad ones] Across the $32$ synthetic runs on the unit square and the one real mesh with a known solution, $I^{\mathrm{BW}}$ stayed above one, with a minimum of $1.004$; Bank–Weiser should therefore not be lumped together with Zienkiewicz–Zhu, which was below one every single time. On the L-shaped domain, however, it is below one on all four meshes, down to $I^{\mathrm{BW}}=0.9935$ (Table 8). The deficit is small, under a percent, and a practitioner would not notice it. The saturation assumption on which reliability rests is not satisfied there, nothing in the computed output says so, and the estimator returns a number that is confidently below the truth. The difference with the equilibrated flux is not that the latter is sharper, but that its failure mode is a certificate one can check (step 4 of Algorithm 7.19) rather than an assumption one must believe.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of assessing the accuracy of finite element simulations performed on irregular or poorly shaped meshes, a common occurrence when dealing with complex geometries. Researchers investigated the applicability of equilibrated flux estimators to provide a computable upper bound on the discretization error, independent of mesh regularity assumptions. The analysis revealed that the error bound is guaranteed and reliable, even with highly distorted elements, relying only on the Poincaré constant related to the cell size. This finding offers a practical tool for quantifying simulation error without strict mesh quality requirements.

fulltext.summary: The study investigates a posteriori error estimation for finite element simulations on meshes with poor geometric quality, specifically addressing scenarios common in real-world applications. Researchers employed equilibrated flux estimators to provide an upper bound on the energy-norm discretization error, demonstrating its reliability even when shape-regularity conditions are not met. Numerical experiments, conducted using FEniCSx, explored the impact of mesh distortion through techniques like vertex displacement and damage introduction, revealing that the estimator's failure mode is pessimism rather than false confidence, with the Bank-Weiser estimator reaching a minimum of 1.004 on synthetic runs.

items.title: A structure-preserving neural density functional for the ions of a polymer electrolyte
items.abstract: Predicting the structure and response of inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes requires a description of ion correlations that retains molecular-scale accuracy while remaining transferable across spatial scales and geometries. We develop a neural density functional for electrolytes that preserves spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability and the Noether identities, with perfect screening recovered in stable, noncritical bulk states. Its nonlinear density dependence captures the concentration-dependent correlations missed by a pair closure, including a crossover from enhanced to suppressed long-wavelength number fluctuations at strong coupling. The functional describes density profiles at an untrained salt concentration and predicts bulk structure factors and the long-wavelength number response. Trained solely on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics, the functional predicts ionic structure in larger domains and in two-dimensional external fields. On the same ion data, it is more accurate than three other neural density-functional architectures and keeps its accuracy with a quarter of the training runs, where the errors of the best alternative grow by about two thirds. The spatial transferability provides a necessary foundation for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions at larger scales.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the behavior of ionic systems within a specific material context, requiring a method that balances computational efficiency with detailed physical representation. Researchers created a novel neural density functional designed to uphold fundamental physical principles and capture complex, nonlinear relationships within the system. Results demonstrate the functional's ability to predict structural properties and responses in new scenarios, outperforming alternative approaches while requiring fewer training iterations. This work highlights a technique for approximating complex systems with a reduced computational burden.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the development of a neural density functional to model ionic systems, employing a force-matching training approach with inverse variance weighting ($w_{r\alpha i}=1/(s_{r\alpha i}^{2}+\bar{s}_{r\alpha}^{2})$) to minimize errors in force density calculations. The functional was trained on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics simulations and demonstrated superior accuracy compared to three alternative architectures, maintaining performance even with a quarter of the training data, achieving profile errors of 1.50% and 3.11% at specific parameters. The method’s transferability was tested on unseen concentrations and in two-dimensional fields, and it showed promise for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions.

items.title: Variational Derivation of the Weak Form for Viscous Flows Involving Free Surfaces with Implications for Geodynamic Simulations
items.abstract: Geodynamic simulations involve solving the Stokes equations, where boundary conditions play a crucial role in governing internal dynamics and surface topography evolution. A common approach is to model the interface in contact with air as a free surface. This interface is stress-free and deforms in response to internal force balances, which is essential for understanding processes ranging from rifted margins to subduction. However, a free surface can introduce instabilities and oscillations in the numerical solution, commonly known as the "drunken sailor" instability, forcing the use of small time steps. Geodynamic models therefore often employ stabilization terms based on the gravitational effect of free-surface motion. To date, these terms have been derived primarily on a heuristic basis. Here, we apply variational calculus to the energy-minimization formulation of incompressible Stokes flow. Using the Gateaux derivative, we derive the complete weak form for a deforming free-surface domain and show that the stabilization terms arise naturally from the free-surface assumption. We consider the linear-viscosity case and identify two boundary-integral contributions: one associated with internal viscous deformation and the other with gravitational body force. Two benchmark cases demonstrate the consistency of the derived formulation with previously proposed stabilization approaches. Our results provide a mathematical foundation for the commonly used gravity stabilization and identify an additional viscous boundary contribution.
excerpts: [6 Numerical Test Cases] Two test cases are considered to assess the accuracy, stability, and applicability of the proposed free-surface stabilization formulations. The tests are arranged in increasing order of physical and numerical complexity. The first case is the Rayleigh–Taylor benchmark and the second test is the Rising Plume test.

[7 Results] Caption: Figure 5: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), defined by Equation ( 70), for the upper surface of the Rayleigh–Taylor instability. The MAE is compared for both full and gravity - only stabilization methods across various time steps and lid viscosities. Both methods demonstrate consistent performance. As expected, the MAE is inversely proportional to lid rigidity, peaking at lower viscosity values where surface deformation is most significant. [A.1 Numerical Workflow and ALE Time Integration] The numerical solution advances in time using an ALE formulation in which the physical velocity and the mesh velocity are treated as distinct quantities. At each time step, the Stokes problem is first solved on the current computational mesh. The resulting physical velocity is then used to determine the motion of selected mesh boundaries through a separate mesh-movement problem. The mesh coordinates are subsequently updated explicitly, and the resulting mesh quality is assessed before proceeding to the next time step. Let $t^{n}$ denote the current time and let $\Delta t^{n}$ be the time-step size. The computational state at time $t^{n}$ consists of the mesh coordinates, the physical fields, and the associated solver and function space definitions. [A.7 Convergence and Verification Procedure] The two analytical benchmarks serve different but complementary purposes. The manufactured-solution benchmark provides a controlled test in which the analytical solution is smooth and known throughout the domain. It therefore establishes the baseline accuracy of the discretization and implementation. The SolVi benchmark adds a strong viscosity contrast and an internal discontinuous interface, providing a more demanding test of the formulation and its treatment of heterogeneous materials. The two tests therefore constitute a progressive verification framework: the manufactured solution establishes baseline numerical accuracy, while the SolVi benchmark evaluates the robustness of the implementation in the presence of strong material heterogeneity and a sharp and well defined internal interface. Together with the ALE mesh-movement and remeshing procedures described above, these benchmarks provide a reproducible framework for assessing the accuracy and numerical reliability of the simulation software.

plain.summary: The study addresses challenges in simulating fluid flows with free surfaces, a common occurrence in geodynamic modeling. Researchers employed variational calculus and the Gateaux derivative to derive a weak form for incompressible Stokes flow within a deforming domain. This derivation revealed the origins of stabilization terms used to mitigate numerical instabilities, specifically identifying contributions from viscous deformation and gravitational forces. The resulting formulation provides a theoretical justification for existing stabilization techniques and highlights a previously overlooked viscous boundary contribution.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the derivation of a weak form for incompressible Stokes flow with a deforming free surface, a common setup in geodynamic simulations. Employing variational calculus and the Gateaux derivative, the authors derive stabilization terms that arise naturally from the free-surface assumption, identifying contributions from both viscous deformation and gravitational body forces. Numerical tests, including the Rayleigh–Taylor instability benchmark and a rising plume test, demonstrate the consistency of the derived formulation with existing stabilization approaches, showing that both full and gravity-only stabilization methods yield comparable mean absolute errors, with the MAE inversely proportional to lid rigidity.

items.title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
items.abstract: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a one-time symbolic phase, the runtime bus-type projection overhead is entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The framework is realized in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 24.4-30.1x faster than the MATPOWER- style baseline and 6.0-7.8x faster than the Schafer-Braun optimized assembly. End-to-end, the grid-level solve time is 11.7x-154.3x faster than pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. Compared with the native C++ LightSim2Grid 1.0.0, grid-level performance is comparable on IEEE 39 and 1.3x-1.8x faster on IEEE 118 and the PEGASE systems. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.
excerpts: [II-B The Power-Flow Equation] Caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed method’s core innovation. By hoisting topology-dependent permutations offline via Theorem 1, the proposed framework eliminates runtime slicing and scattered writes, condensing the traditional loop into a single-pass direct-fill stream to achieve up to 21 $\times$ speedup and outperform the state-of-the-art open-source C++ solver.

[III-A Non-Holomorphic Deadlock and the Dual Real-Mapping Paradigm] Redundant Differentiation: Wasting significant CPU cycles and arithmetic throughput evaluating derivatives for dropped states (e.g., slack and PV bus voltage magnitudes) that are subsequently discarded. Indirect Spatial Partitioning: Relying on extensive layout-mapping tables to index and route derivatives into traditional $\bm{J}_{11}$ through $\bm{J}_{22}$ sub-blocks, introducing severe pointer-dereferencing and indirection overheads inside the iteration loop. Non-Contiguous Scatter Assembly: Enforcing dimensional reduction via scattered writes that distribute values across disjoint matrix segments, which completely disrupts hardware prefetching, invalidates CPU cache lines, and severely limits parallel scalability. These limitations transform the iteration hot path into a performance graveyard of branch mispredictions and cache invalidations, which also significantly lower the parallel efficiency on modern CPUs and GPUs.

[V-A Experimental Setup] Results are averaged over seven batches of 300 solves. We compare these paths against pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba [ 14 ] and LightSim2Grid 1.0.0 [ 15 ]. LightSim2Grid uses a C++ backend on a pre-built model. Given the rapid evolution of power-flow software, comparisons are performed using fixed software releases. The iteration loop timings in Table IV are averages of 20 repeated complete power-flow solves after warm-up, with initialized network models and cached solver data reused and the initial voltage reset for each solve.

plain.summary: The work addresses the significant computational cost associated with Jacobian matrix assembly in iterative optimization algorithms. A novel approach is presented that leverages symbolic permutation and algebraic equivariance to streamline the Jacobian construction process, eliminating runtime overhead and enabling a single-pass algorithm. Experimental results on various power system test cases demonstrate substantial speedups compared to existing methods, with improvements ranging from 6x to over 150x in grid-level solve times. The technique's applicability extends beyond power flow analysis to related network optimization problems.

fulltext.summary: The paper addresses the computational expense of Jacobian matrix assembly within Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis, a process traditionally hindered by repeated calculations and inefficient memory access patterns. The authors introduce a symbolic-permutation-based method that pre-calculates topological permutations to eliminate runtime overhead and fuse differentiation and assembly into a single, branchless operation. Experiments using IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate a 21x speedup compared to a C++ solver and significant performance gains over existing open-source tools, with grid-level solve times improved by factors of 11.7x to 154.3x. The technique is presented as extensible to other network-based problems like transient stability analysis.

items.title: Linear and entropy-stable scheme for the dynamic van der Waals model of non-isothermal liquid-vapor flows
items.abstract: In this paper, we propose a linear and decoupled fully discrete scheme that preserves the entropy production property for the dynamic van der Waals model. This model provides a thermodynamically consistent diffuse-interface framework for describing non-isothermal phase transitions in single-component liquid-vapor systems, containing the coupled conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy. We first introduce an equivalent reformulation of the governing equations that avoids the use of chain-rule identities, which generally fail under discrete differentiation. Further, a component-wise convex-splitting method is employed to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature. This treatment provides a discrete entropy-stable inequality without a time step restriction. Based on the explicitly treated velocity, the scheme allows the three conservation equations to be solved linearly and sequentially in a decoupled manner. Since the momentum equation does not directly affect the entropy-stability analysis, we use a classical linear semi-implicit scheme to solve it. Numerical experiments verify the expected numerical accuracy. Simulations of droplet evaporation and two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects further demonstrate the proposed method can capture complex non-isothermal phase-transition dynamics while numerically reproducing the discrete entropy production behavior.

[5 Conclusion] A major feature of the proposed method is that it preserves the entropy-production law at the fully discrete level, which is one of the fundamental thermodynamic structures of the model. Numerical experiments verify the expected first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy and further demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively capture droplet evaporation, two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects. These results indicate that the scheme is robust, efficient, and physically consistent. Future work will mainly focus on two directions. One is the generalization of the numerical scheme to complex models, such as thermodynamically consistent boundary conditions and multi-component flows. The other is the development of fully discrete schemes that simultaneously maintain entropy production and energy conservation, with additional attention to positivity preservation of density and temperature.

plain.summary: The study addresses the simulation of phase transitions in fluids by developing a numerical scheme for a specific thermodynamic model. Researchers reformulated governing equations and utilized a convex-splitting method to ensure entropy stability during discretization, avoiding issues with discrete differentiation. The resulting scheme allows for a decoupled, linear solution of conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, which was validated through simulations of droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects. The work demonstrates the scheme's ability to accurately capture complex dynamics while maintaining numerical stability.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces a new numerical scheme for simulating dynamic van der Waals models describing non-isothermal phase transitions. The scheme employs a component-wise convex-splitting method to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature, ensuring entropy stability without time step restrictions. Numerical simulations, including droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects, were performed on a domain of size L=100 with a radius of R=0.5, demonstrating first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy based on Cauchy difference calculations.

items.title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
items.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
excerpts: [IV-B Comparative Strategies for Limited Memory (Original Contribution)] To simulate the constrained environment of an embedded device (e.g., limited RAM) and allow the algorithm to process large datasets sequentially, we compared three learning strategies: Reference Method (Full Memory): Processing the entire dataset at once (infeasible on microcontrollers). Simple Block Processing: Iterative processing using fixed-size data buffers $W$ (e.g., 1024 lines). This simulates diversity by simply moving to a new block. Block Processing with Explicit Diversity Management (Proposed Method): This innovative strategy explicitly manages the buffer content to ensure diversity. The buffer is filled. The buffer is sorted (e.g., based on accMotion value), complexity $O(W\log W)$. Only samples at the extremities of the distribution (e.g., the lower and upper halves) are retained to maximize sample diversity. The resulting empty spaces are refilled with new data. The GHA step is executed on this diversified buffer.

[V-B K-MEANS Clustering for Activity Analysis] The differences between the results in C++ and Python programs can be attributed to several factors. The C++ program processes the data in blocks of 1024 rows, while the Python program processes the data sequentially. This may affect how the eigenvalues and eigenvectors are updated. The initial parameters, such as the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, may be initialized differently in the two programs, which may influence the final results. The C++ program uses an online approach to update the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, while the Python program uses a batch approach. This may lead to differences in the convergence of the results. The Python program ignores rows without payload, which can reduce the number of data rows processed, while the C++ program does not seem to have this logic. The C++ program normalizes the data by ignoring some columns (1, 3, and 6), while the Python program normalizes all columns. This can lead to differences in the values of the processed data.

[VI-A Inherent Limitations of the Proposed Methodology] We detail the disadvantages and limitations of the proposed approach, as required by the critiques (Critique 2): PCA Linearity Limit: PCA (and GHA) is a linear method. It can only capture linear relationships between variables. If data relationships are non-linear, this method may not capture the true structure. Information Loss: Dimensionality reduction entails an inevitable loss of total variance. Implementation and Performance Cost: The explicit memory management strategy (sorting) increases the implementation complexity and the time complexity to $O(W\log W)$ per iteration, which affects speed on low-power devices. Dependency on Sorting Criterion: The success of the diversity preservation method relies heavily on choosing the correct variable for sorting (e.g., accMotion). A poor choice could compromise the preservation of diversity. Ecosystem Compatibility: There is a recognized time lag in algorithm development between microcontroller ecosystems (ARDUINO and Micropython).

plain.summary: The study addresses the design of distributed computing architectures for real-time data processing in building automation systems. Researchers developed a framework utilizing low-power microcontrollers and a lightweight orchestration system to manage data acquisition, storage, and processing. A modified version of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm was implemented for dimensionality reduction, demonstrating comparable results to full-memory processing despite increased computational complexity due to sorting operations.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a system for data acquisition and processing within smart buildings, focusing on resource-constrained environments. A Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) is adapted for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low-power microcontrollers, employing a block processing strategy with explicit diversity management through sorting, resulting in a time complexity of O(W log W). Experimental validation using Tour Perret sensor data demonstrated that this approach achieves visually equivalent results to full-memory processing while identifying two distinct operational states.

items.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
items.abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.
excerpts: Caption: Figure 1: The overall workflow of PDE-PFN. Our model performs in-context learning (ICL) based on given observations (i.e., context) to infer solutions. At inference, PDE-PFN conditions on observations from the target instance without separate operator-level demonstrations or target-instance gradient updates. Even when trained with an approximated PINN prior, our method can improve over noisy approximate pretraining data.

[4.1 Experimental Setup] We consider a family of 2D CDR equations with three reaction terms as the pre-training dataset. This family is constructed from equations with coefficient dictionary ( [formula]), resulting in a total of 2,187 unique PDEs. They are simulated from the same initial condition, which allows differences in the resulting dynamics to stem solely from the variations in coefficients. For PINN prior, each PINN is trained independently, and its predicted solutions are used as noisy priors. On average, the generated PINN priors exhibit an $L_{2}$ relative error of 0.02280. For cross-PDE transfer experiments, we employ the SWE and CNSE datasets from PDEBench [ 47 ]. These two equations are chosen because they are commonly used to validate PDE solvers in SciML. Both datasets consist of 1,000 samples generated from distinct initial conditions. The SWE dataset contains a single feature, the water height, whereas the CNSE dataset includes $x$ - and $y$ -velocities, pressure, and density. Detailed information on the datasets can be found in Appendix B.

[4.3 Cross-PDE Transfer after Fine-tuning] Caption: Table 5: The evaluation results for the operator learning task applied to CNSE. The best performance is marked in bold and the second-best performance is marked with underline. The experimental results in Table 5 show that both versions of our model outperform the baselines on two relative error metrics. Notably, although DPOT’s pre-training corpus already includes the CNSE dataset from PDEBench, our models still achieve superior performance over DPOT on both metrics. While DPOT was originally evaluated on predicting one time step ahead, in our setting the task was extended to predicting up to four time steps ahead. As a result, DPOT exhibited lower performance than reported in the original paper. These results support cross-PDE transfer after fine-tuning for multivariate trajectory prediction.

[H.3 Test-Time Prediction with Biased Context Noise in the 2D CDR Family] Since Theorem A.2 assumes unbiased noise, we further investigate how robust our model remains when the inference stage includes biased Gaussian noise added to the analytic solution. We set the standard deviation of Gaussian noise to $\sigma=0.01$ and vary only the magnitude of the bias. The evaluation is performed on the temporal extrapolation task of the 2D CDR equations, using the $L_{2}$ relative error for comparison. Caption: Table 10: The evaluation results for the temporal extrapolation tasks applied to the family of 2D CDR equations. They are measured at the seen coefficients ( [formula]). The experimental results in Table 10 show that when the bias is below 3%, the performance degradation remains relatively minor compared to the bias level. However, once the bias reaches approximately 3% or higher, the error begins to increase more noticeably. This indicates that PDE-PFN maintains robustness against moderate systematic bias, but large bias eventually leads to a degradation in accuracy as expected.

plain.summary: This work investigates a novel neural network architecture for solving partial differential equations, drawing inspiration from large language models and a specific inference mechanism called posterior predictive mean-based inference. The proposed method, PDE-PFN, utilizes a Transformer-based architecture pre-trained on approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks to enable in-context learning and prediction. Experiments across various PDEs demonstrate the model's ability to generalize to new equations, maintain robustness with noisy data, and perform inference without gradient updates, ultimately achieving competitive predictive accuracy.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces PDE-PFN, a neural solver that leverages in-context learning inspired by prior-data fitted networks to predict PDE solutions. The model is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and utilizes Transformer architectures with self- and cross-attention mechanisms. Experiments on 2D CDR equations and datasets like SWE and CNSE demonstrate PDE-PFN's ability to generalize across different equations and maintain accuracy even with noisy or biased priors, achieving relative $L_2$ errors as low as 0.02280 with the PINN prior.

items.title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
items.abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.
excerpts: [3 Method: Multi-agent LLM framework] The detailed prompt retains these elements and adds a structured Chain-of-Thought procedure and a list of method classes specified by the Human Researcher for systematic exploration. Each hypothesis is assigned to one principal class, which is also stored in its experiment-log record, and the log is converted into a dynamically updated coverage map. For every class, the map reports the number of evaluated hypotheses, the best metric value, and a coverage status such as “not explored,” “limited data,” or “explored.” The map is included in the next Analyst prompt, which prioritizes suitable classes with little or no coverage and revisits an explored class only when a substantially different hypothesis is proposed. This mechanism structures an open natural-language search without reducing it to a finite list of implementations. The task-specific prompt configurations are described in Section 4; the detailed-mode prompt materials are provided in Supplementary Materials.

[4 Experimental setup] The same framework is applied to five tasks with different types of information representation: two spiking-network classification tasks, two boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and one boundary-value problem for the generalized Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

[4.5 Evaluation protocol] In the single-soliton problem, the identity-map baselines give $\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=4.69\cdot 10^{-2}$, $5.51\cdot 10^{-2}$, and $4.85\cdot 10^{-2}$ in the Sonar, Claude, and Qwen agent runs, respectively. In the GNLSE problem with a Gaussian perturbation, the corresponding single-run baselines give $\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=1.28\cdot 10^{-1}$, $2.15\cdot 10^{-1}$, and $1.85\cdot 10^{-1}$; over $n=10$ additional baseline trainings, mean is $\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=(1.65\pm 0.18)\cdot 10^{-1}$ (Table 11). In the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, the baseline gives $\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=1.41\cdot 10^{-3}$ and $\Delta_{m}^{(u)}=9.31\cdot 10^{-2}$. The SNN baseline (argmax over output spike rates, without Gaussian receptive fields (GRF) or bagging) gives an accuracy of 79.88 % on MNIST and 90.83 % on digits, consistent with previously published results Sboev et al. (2025). The gap between the datasets motivated target accuracies of 90 % on MNIST and 93 % on digits.

[8 Limitations] Despite the results reported above, the present study has several limitations that should be taken into account when interpreting the findings and when comparing our system with alternative approaches. Restricted search space. The agent modifies a fixed catalogue of editable blocks (encoders, neuron models, connectivity schemes for SNNs; loss weights, activation functions and sampling strategies for PINNs). Structural transformations that fall outside this catalogue – for example, adding auxiliary networks or replacing the entire training paradigm – cannot be discovered by the current agent and would require an extended action space. Flat experiment log without a hypothesis graph. The Recorder stores runs as a chronological JSON log; it does not maintain a directed acyclic graph of hypotheses and their dependencies. As a consequence, the Analyst re-derives relations between experiments from the log at every step, which limits the depth of multi-step reasoning that can be sustained over long sessions.

plain.summary: The work investigates a method for automating the optimization of specific components within machine learning models, moving beyond full script optimization or discrete architectural searches. A multi-agent large language model system is developed, with distinct roles for analysis, code generation, and record-keeping, operating within a constrained code space. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through two applications: optimizing a spiking neural network for classification and solving differential equations using a specific type of neural network. The results show significant improvements in classification accuracy and error reduction across several benchmark problems.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed to automatically tune components within existing machine learning models, operating within a semantically constrained space. The framework utilizes an analyst, coder, and recorder agent, employing a Chain-of-Thought procedure and a structured experiment log to systematically explore potential improvements. The approach was tested on spiking neural network classification tasks and boundary-value problems, including solving high-order differential equations using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, achieving significant performance gains over baseline methods, such as a 2491-fold reduction in error for the single-soliton problem. The authors acknowledge limitations, noting the restricted search space and lack of a hypothesis graph within the framework.

items.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
items.abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.
excerpts: [2 Turbulence Through the Lens of Complexity] By explicitly distinguishing the disorganized stochastic regime (Regime II) from structurally emergent dynamics (Regime IV), this taxonomy demystifies the generalization crisis in data-driven turbulence modeling. It demonstrates that ML-RANS failures in complex flows are not caused by algorithmic limitations or insufficient training data, but by the fundamental misapplication of statistical tools to structurally emergent regimes where non-Markovian memory effects physically invalidate local closure.

[2.1 The Flow-Dependent Nature of Emergent Memory] This establishes a firm theoretical boundary on purely data-driven closures. An ML model optimized over a finite database constructs an approximation $K_{\theta}=\mathcal{ML}(\mathcal{D}_{\rm train})$. While this surrogate may interpolate within the sampled manifold, it cannot mathematically guarantee extrapolation to unseen instability mechanisms. The challenge in Regime IV is not insufficient data, but the impossibility of learning a universal mapping for a highly flow-specific, emergent quantity. Consequently, the most robust strategy is not to model this history dependence, but to dynamically resolve the memory-bearing coherent structures via scale-resolving simulations (SRS).

[3 Statistical Learning in Emergent Regimes] Physically, $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}\mid\bm{\mu},\mathcal{F}_{k}]$ is the true Reynolds stress, $\mathbf{y}_{k}$, for geometry $k$. The term $P(\mathcal{F}_{k}\mid\bm{\mu})$ acts as a statistical weight, $w_{k}$, reflecting how frequently the local state $\bm{\mu}$ appears in geometry $k$ during training. The optimal prediction therefore reduces to a weighted average: For structurally non-injective flows, this mathematical compromise produces a smeared stress tensor that satisfies no valid governing equations. The resulting Bayes error is irreducible. Increasing training data diversity merely incorporates more incompatible mappings into the mixture, exacerbating the error. Thus, poor generalization in Regime IV stems from the fundamental absence of a well-defined functional relationship, not limited model capacity. In out-of-distribution applications ( $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{test}}$), these flaws are severely magnified. Because standard neural networks learn statistical correlations rather than invariant causal relationships [ 12, 13 ], they lack the physical mechanisms to extrapolate across global context changes, yielding uncontrolled errors.

[Outlook] Achieving optimal outcomes in data-driven turbulence modeling requires pivoting from universal, one-size-fits-all closures toward situation-aware AI/ML deployment. Conceptually, this perspective advances the field by grounding ML learnability in complex-systems theory and non-equilibrium physics, demystifying why data-driven surrogates fail in memory-bearing regimes. Practically, it proposes a physics-based recipe for flow-aware simulation parameterized by $SK/\epsilon$, enabling researchers to avoid misapplying ML-RANS while optimizing computational expenditure in scale-resolving simulations. Crucially, this qualitative framework sets the stage for establishing precise quantitative threshold values of $SK/\epsilon$. Preliminary work [ 14 ] leverages non-equilibrium thermodynamics [ 15 ] toward this goal, laying the groundwork for an AI adjudicator capable of evaluating flow states in situ to dynamically select physically valid, computationally optimal modeling strategies.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenges of integrating AI/ML techniques into turbulence modeling, noting limitations in both data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and scale-resolving simulation (SRS) approaches. Researchers developed a turbulence taxonomy map using a complexity framework based on Reynolds number and non-equilibrium parameters to guide the appropriate application of different AI/ML methods. The resulting classification identifies specific regimes where physics-informed neural networks offer a particularly effective solution, alongside guidance for when other approaches are more suitable.

fulltext.summary: The paper addresses the challenges of applying machine learning to turbulence modeling, specifically highlighting the limitations of data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) and scale-resolving simulations (SRS). It proposes a turbulence taxonomy map based on the Reynolds number ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$) to guide the optimal deployment of AI/ML techniques, distinguishing between regimes where ML-RANS can generalize and those requiring explicit scale resolution. The authors argue that failures in complex flows stem from misapplying statistical tools to regimes with non-Markovian memory effects, and suggest physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective in specific areas of this taxonomy.

items.title: PINNs for N=2* holography
items.abstract: Can a holographic theory be reconstructed from its equation of state? We investigate this question using physics-informed neural networks in the bosonic-mass sector of the Pilch--Warner model. We first validate the PINN approach against an analytic solution encoding the leading high-temperature corrections to the conformal equation of state. We then reconstruct nonlinear black-brane geometries and the scalar potential using thermodynamics, ultraviolet asymptotics, Ward identities, and horizon regularity. Independent solutions of the bulk Einstein-scalar equations demonstrate that accurately reproducing thermodynamics with a trained PINN does not guarantee an accurate reconstruction of the scalar potential. High-precision knowledge of the high-temperature equation of state constrains nonlinear interactions in the bulk scalar potential. Fixing the cubic coupling to its exact PW value, motivated by this high-temperature extraction, reduces the maximum sampled error in the reconstructed scalar self-interactions by a factor of $\sim 15$ compared with constraining only the bulk scalar mass. plain.summary: The study explores the potential of using machine learning techniques to derive physical systems from thermodynamic constraints. Researchers employed a neural network architecture trained on known data to generate solutions for geometric configurations and energy landscapes. The investigation revealed that precise thermodynamic information is crucial for accurately reconstructing certain aspects of the system, and incorporating additional physical properties like viscosity significantly improves the reconstruction's fidelity. Ultimately, the work demonstrates a pathway for extracting detailed information about a physical system's internal structure from macroscopic observations.

fulltext.summary: The study explores the reconstruction of holographic theories using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) within the Pilch-Warner (PW) model's bosonic-mass sector. Researchers validated the PINN approach against an analytic solution for high-temperature corrections to the conformal equation of state, then attempted to reconstruct black-brane geometries and scalar potentials based on thermodynamic constraints, ultraviolet asymptotics, and horizon regularity. The networks, trained with 1,166,422 updates over twelve hours on a Quadro RTX 5000, utilized Chebyshev nodes for collocation points and achieved a 15-fold reduction in error for reconstructed scalar self-interactions when the cubic coupling was fixed to its PW value, with an additional 13-fold reduction when bulk viscosity was also incorporated.

items.title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
items.abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.
