plain.summary: This work addresses stochastic boundary-value problems where the governing operator is itself random, presenting a novel neural network architecture to model this scenario. The approach utilizes a stochastic neural network with a random structure defined by a latent Gaussian field and a Poisson point process on a manifold, driven by a shared stochastic process. Training involves minimizing a combined objective function that balances data fidelity with alignment to the problem's conditional distribution, ultimately producing a network capable of representing non-Gaussian random operators. The method is demonstrated on an elliptic problem and proposes a generalized-posterior formulation for hyperparameter inference.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) to address stochastic boundary-value problems with random operators. The method employs a non-feedforward, intrinsically random neural network architecture where neuron locations and connectivity are determined by a latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a multiply connected manifold. Training involves a supervised objective combining data fidelity and cross-entropy alignment, using a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, and is demonstrated on a stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface. The authors evaluate the method’s performance using a continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) diagnostic, finding that the SNN incurs approximately 10% more CRPS than a data-driven benchmark in the misspecified regime.

items.title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
items.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
excerpts: [I Introduction] The remaining sections are organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details our proposed methodology, including the formulation of the Markov Decision Process (MDP) for image captioning, the design of the reward function, and the modeling of reinforcement learning networks, followed by fine-tuning the model through solving the MDP with RL. Section 4 presents the experimental results, and Section 5 reports the ablation studies. Section 6 provides discussions, while Section 7 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

[IV-A Experimental Settings] Datasets: We consider both a sparse-object dataset (COCO) [ 43 ] and a dense-object dataset (Visual Genome) [ 31 ]. To prepare datasets for LVLM fine-tuning, we randomly augment each image with captioning instructions, as detailed in the Appendix C. For COCO, we adopt the CHAIR metric, which is specifically designed for this dataset and ensures the reliable, consistent evaluation of hallucination. For Visual Genome, we employ CCEval [ 91 ], an extension of CHAIR that leverages LLM-assisted object extraction to better capture objects beyond the COCO objects, making it well-suited for the Visual Genome benchmark.

[IV-B Experimental Results] Additionally, our method is able to maintain or enhance caption quality across various metrics. Table III presents our results. The row Ours demonstrates the use of OCS and KL divergence, maintaining performance comparable to the base model, InstructBLIP. There is a slight increase in SPICE, BLUE, and BERTScore, which we attribute to the generated captions being more factual, concise, and focused, resulting in shorter and more precise outputs. When ground truth captions are available, incorporating METEOR and BERTScore, as in Ours+, significantly improves caption quality. It is evident that Ours+ significantly improves captioning performance across SPICE, BLEU, and BERTScore, surpassing all previous baselines. Extend evaluations to more complex dataset: We evaluate our model on the Visual Genome dataset using the CCEval metric from Halle-switch [ 91 ] to assess its performance in more complex settings with denser object in the image.

[VII Limitations and Future Directions] While our framework effectively mitigates object hallucination, several limitations remain. First, OCS is currently defined over object sets and therefore primarily targets object-level hallucination. Hallucinations involving incorrect attributes (e.g., color) or relations (e.g., spatial or interaction errors) are not explicitly optimized. However, since OCS is fundamentally a precision–recall (F1-based) formulation, it can be extended to structured units such as (object, attribute) pairs or (subject, relation, object) triplets, provided reliable automatic extraction is available. Exploring such extensions is an important direction for future work. Second, in real-world deployment settings where ground-truth annotations are unavailable, hallucination mitigation depends on the coverage and accuracy of the object detector used to construct visual object sets. Detectors limited to fixed vocabularies (e.g., COCO’s 80 classes) may leave non-COCO hallucinations undetected. Integrating open-vocabulary detection models could further improve robustness in real-world applications.

plain.summary: The study investigates a method for improving the accuracy of image captioning models, which sometimes fabricate objects not present in the image. Researchers developed a reinforcement learning approach that uses automated language metrics to guide the model's learning process, reducing the need for human feedback. This framework incorporates a novel consistency score and regularization techniques to ensure stability and prevent undesirable behaviors during training. The resulting model demonstrated a significant reduction in hallucinated objects while also improving overall caption quality.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a reinforcement learning framework to reduce object hallucination in image captioning models. The approach uses an Object Consistency Score (OCS) and KL-regularization within a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) variant, fine-tuning adapters on a frozen LVLM backbone. Experiments on COCO and Visual Genome datasets demonstrate a reduction of up to 41% in hallucination using the CHAIR and CCEval metrics, respectively, while also improving caption quality with metrics like BERTScore and METEOR.

items.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
items.abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

The authors develop a variational formulation that combines data with PDE constraints, using energy regularization and debiasing techniques to improve generalization. Their analysis reveals anisotropic behavior in learning parabolic PDEs, leading to rate-optimal estimation and generalization error bounds that depend on temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. items.title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
items.abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

Researchers developed a process combining symbolic regression, mathematical validation, and large language model ranking to identify potential growth laws. Results demonstrated that while the AI-assisted workflow can produce plausible trajectories and explanations, incorporating physics-informed neural network refitting sometimes worsened the accuracy of the recovered growth law, highlighting the importance of careful evaluation beyond predictive performance.

items.abstract: Artificial dissipation improves the robustness of high-order methods for under-resolved flows, but can compromise accuracy and suppress physically relevant structures if its strength and spatial distribution are not appropriately controlled. We present a sensor-activated nonlinear artificial-dissipation framework, inspired by the residual correction method, for continuous and discontinuous summation-by-parts discretizations. In contrast to many existing spectral-element dissipation operators that either reduce the formal order of accuracy or target only the highest polynomial modes, the proposed framework permits design- and higher-order dissipation with explicit control over its magnitude, spatial distribution, activation, and convergence rate under mesh refinement. This modular construction also recovers several existing methods through appropriate choices of its components. The dissipation preserves discrete conservation and semidiscrete entropy stability whenever the base method satisfies these properties. It is dimensionally consistent, element local, and discretization agnostic, as the added term is constructed independently of the base spatial residual. For smooth solutions under suitable mesh assumptions, we establish parameter choices that retain the formal accuracy of the base discretization. Numerical experiments with summation-by-parts discretizations of the Burgers and Euler equations demonstrate substantially improved robustness for under-resolved flows and flows with shock waves while retaining high-order accuracy for smooth solutions, using the same parameter choices across several test problems. Overall, these results show that targeted dissipation can improve the robustness of high-order methods without excessive damping of resolved flow structures.

The two- and three-dimensional isentropic vortex tests examine smooth-solution accuracy, conservation, and entropy dissipation, while the Kelvin–Helmholtz tests assess robustness for under-resolved vortical flows. The Burgers, Sod, Shu–Osher, and two-dimensional Riemann problems assess the performance of the proposed dissipation for solutions containing shocks. With a kinetic-energy-preserving base volume flux, the Taylor–Green vortex tests assess the influence of the added dissipation on kinetic-energy evolution. The same dissipation parameter-selection rules are used across the test problems. The paper is organized as follows. Sections 2 and 3 present the preliminaries and base discretizations. plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of maintaining stability in numerical simulations of fluid dynamics when using high-order discretization schemes. Researchers developed a new artificial dissipation method that dynamically adjusts its strength based on the solution's behavior, aiming to improve robustness without sacrificing accuracy. The method's design allows for control over its spatial distribution and activation, preserving desirable properties of the underlying discretization, and demonstrating improved performance in simulations of the Burgers and Euler equations.

fulltext.summary: The paper addresses the challenges of maintaining robustness and accuracy when using high-order numerical methods for solving hyperbolic conservation laws. It introduces a novel, sensor-activated nonlinear artificial dissipation framework for summation-by-parts discretizations, drawing inspiration from residual correction methods. The method is designed to be element-local and discretization-agnostic, allowing for controlled dissipation strength and spatial distribution while preserving discrete conservation and entropy stability, and it was assessed using the Burgers and Euler equations in two and three dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrated improved robustness for under-resolved flows, particularly in the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability test, where computations with the proposed dissipation reached a final time of 15, whereas those with only interface dissipation failed by time 5.34.

items.abstract: We establish a strong convergence rate for the implicit midpoint method applied to the periodic stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equation with additive noise, addressing a question that has remained open since the work of Debussche and Printems. To control nonlinear error growth, we obtain exponential integrability estimates for the exact and comparison solutions using the coercivity of a classical KdV invariant. We then derive local error bounds from estimates for the comparison solutions and control error accumulation through an $L^2$ error propagation identity that isolates a martingale increment. Under $H_0^{9/2}$ regularity assumptions on the noise and the deterministic initial data, we prove that, on every fixed finite time interval, the maximum $L^2(\mathbb{T})$ error at the time points is $O(h)$ in $L^p(Ω)$ for every $1\le p<\infty$. Notably, the exponential integrability and the convergence rate hold for every damping coefficient $λ\ge0$, including the undamped case $λ=0$. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted first-order convergence.

plain.summary: The study investigates the behavior of a specific numerical scheme for solving a nonlinear stochastic partial differential equation. Researchers developed new mathematical tools, including exponential integrability estimates and an error propagation identity, to analyze the accuracy of the implicit midpoint method. The analysis demonstrates a first-order convergence rate for the method, meaning the error decreases proportionally to the step size, and this result is validated through computational experiments. The findings extend previous work by providing a more complete understanding of the method's performance under various conditions.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates the strong convergence rate of the implicit midpoint method for solving the periodic stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equation, a nonlinear partial differential equation. The authors derive error bounds using exponential integrability estimates and an $L^2$ error propagation identity, establishing a first-order convergence rate of $O(h)$ in $L^p(Ω)$ for $1\le p<\infty$. Numerical experiments, performed with a Fourier pseudospectral method and fixed-point iteration, confirm the theoretical predictions for various damping coefficients and demonstrate convergence rates close to one.

items.title: Provable Method of Moments for Cryo-EM
items.abstract: We study the recovery of a three-dimensional volume in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) from noisy tomographic projections acquired at unknown viewing rotations, drawn independently and uniformly from $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. We show that, in a spherical-shell representation satisfying an explicit shell-separation condition, the first three moments generically determine the underlying real volume up to its intrinsic global $\mathrm{O}(3)$ ambiguity. The proof is constructive and yields a frequency-marching procedure that successively recovers the volume. Consequently, consistent recovery in the high-noise regime has sample complexity $n=ω(σ^6)$, where $n$ is the number of observations and $σ^2$ is the noise variance. Numerical experiments validate the constructive recovery scheme under finite sampling and additive noise, and indicate that direct third-moment optimization can succeed beyond the structural assumptions required by the constructive proof.

plain.summary: The work addresses the reconstruction of a 3D volume from a set of projections, where the projections are noisy and acquired at random orientations. A theoretical framework is developed based on the analysis of moments, demonstrating that the first three moments uniquely define the volume under specific conditions. The authors provide a constructive recovery algorithm and analyze its sample complexity, showing a dependence on the noise variance, and support their findings with numerical simulations.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a method for reconstructing a three-dimensional volume from noisy tomographic projections in cryo-electron microscopy, employing a constructive recovery scheme based on the first three projected moments. The method represents the volume on spherical Fourier shells and uses a frequency-marching procedure to recover coefficients, with a forward march isolating outer-shell coefficients and a reverse backfill completing the reconstruction. Numerical experiments, performed on synthetic signals and molecular volumes like TRPV1 and the 80S ribosome, demonstrate the method's performance and suggest that direct third-moment optimization can succeed even beyond the structural assumptions of the constructive proof, achieving convergence to similar solutions across multiple random initializations.

items.title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
items.abstract: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

plain.summary: The study addresses the computational expense associated with simulating turbulent flow phenomena, specifically focusing on a configuration involving buoyancy-driven convection. Researchers employed a parallel spectral deferred correction method to advance the solution in time, aiming to improve the efficiency of direct numerical simulations. Results demonstrated that this approach facilitated increased temporal resolution and parallelization, ultimately reducing the overall simulation time. The work highlights a strategy for managing the computational demands of complex fluid dynamics problems.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a method for accelerating direct numerical simulations of Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a turbulent flow model. Researchers employed parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method, implemented in both pySDC (GPU-supported) and dedalus (CPU-based) codes, to reduce simulation time. Results on JUSUF and JUPITER systems demonstrated that parallel SDC can improve concurrency and allow for larger stable time steps, leading to a reduction in wall-clock time per free-fall time, with parallel efficiencies reaching approximately 80% for certain configurations.

items.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
items.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

plain.summary: The study investigates the origins of scale inconsistencies in Transformer architectures, proposing a new framework called Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA) inspired by physical dimensional analysis. NDA defines neural units to govern tensor rescaling and addition, enabling the creation of a unit-consistent multi-loss objective and a novel architecture, the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT). Experiments on language models and other architectures demonstrate that GCT exhibits improved training stability, robustness to quantization, and overall performance compared to existing methods.

fulltext.summary: The paper introduces Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a framework for ensuring scale consistency in neural networks, using a formalism inspired by physics. The approach involves defining "neural units" and employing dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) to diagnose scale mismatches, culminating in the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) architecture. Experiments with GCT on language models, vision tasks, and a limited set of physics-informed neural network (PINN) problems demonstrate improved stability and robustness to quantization, achieving a 124M validation loss of 3.903 nats.

items.title: Numerical simulation of biological capsules based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes
items.abstract: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for the simulation of biological capsules based on meshes that adapt iteration-wise to the shape of the membrane. The discretization leverages a Hybrid High Order method (HHO) to solve a Stokes problem with a source term distributed on the interface between the internal and the external phases. The HHO discretization supports meshes composed of general polygons, permitting to use fitted meshes that can be easily generated by cutting the elements intersected by the interface. Moreover, polygonal meshes allow arbitrarily accurate interface discretizations without introducing bulk degrees of freedom. The presentation of the simulation algorithm is completed with a proof-of-concept numerical test on a well-established benchmark: the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow.

Sliver cuts are, however, the crucial challenge in the design of unfitted high-order schemes such as Cut-FEM or Cut-HHO, which typically rely on specific techniques, such as Ghost Penalty, to enforce stability [ Burman et al., 2015; Burman and Ern, 2019 ]. [Conclusion and Perspectives] In this work, we have proposed a novel approach for the simulation of capsule dynamics based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes, summarized in Algorithm 1. The methodology leverages a Hybrid High Order discretization for flow equations supporting polygonal meshes. The flexibility of the method in terms of mesh requirements allows to treat in a straightforward way the interface conditions associated to the fluid-structure interaction while keeping the overhead linked to mesh adaptation moderate. As a proof of concept, the performance of the polygonal interface-fitted approach has been tested successfully on a simple yet paradigmatic benchmark featuring a capsule undergoing moderate to strong deformation in shear flow.

plain.summary: The study addresses the computational modeling of deformable objects with distinct internal and external environments. A novel numerical method, termed Hybrid High Order, is employed to solve fluid dynamics equations on meshes that dynamically adjust to the object's boundary. The method utilizes polygonal elements, enabling precise representation of the interface and avoiding unnecessary computational complexity in the bulk fluid domain. Results are validated through a comparison with a standard benchmark problem involving the deformation of a capsule in a shear flow.

fulltext.summary: The work introduces a numerical framework for simulating biological capsules using a Hybrid High Order (HHO) method to solve a Stokes problem on interface-fitted polygonal meshes. The simulation, implemented using the Python package polymemb and solved with a Sequential Least Square Programming (SLSQP) algorithm, was tested on a capsule undergoing deformation in a shear flow, demonstrating accurate reproduction of the capsule's trajectory. The authors note that sliver cuts in the mesh can occasionally degrade accuracy, but the impact on the trajectory appears minimal in the tested configuration, achieving a maximum deformation and tilting angle comparable to results from IBM-based solvers.

items.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
items.abstract: Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.

plain.summary: The study addresses the problem of estimating parameters within compartmental models of infectious diseases, which are often characterized by linear relationships. A novel approach, physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), is introduced to fit these parameters, eliminating the need for data derivatives and jointly estimating the initial state. The method incorporates split conformal prediction to provide distribution-free uncertainty quantification and achieves significantly improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing techniques, demonstrating substantial error reduction and high coverage rates across various benchmark models.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses parameter estimation in compartment models of infectious diseases, employing a regression framework where the model's derivative is linear in the parameters. The method, termed Physics-informed Weak Regression (PIWR), integrates the model in time, jointly estimating the initial state and achieving high-order accuracy without requiring derivatives of the data. PIWR demonstrates improved accuracy compared to Disease-informed Neural Networks (DINNs) and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), achieving up to four orders of magnitude better results in some cases and requiring significantly less computation time.

items.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.

plain.summary: The study addresses the difficulty of accurately capturing derivatives when using neural networks to solve parametric partial differential equations. A novel neural network architecture, BeTINN, is proposed, combining structured conditional parameterization with time-parameter conditioning to improve adaptability. The method was tested on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, demonstrating enhanced accuracy in both solution values and sensitivities compared to existing approaches. The research also highlights the complexities of evaluating derivative accuracy in physics-informed neural network training.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the challenge of accurately solving parametric partial differential equations, specifically the Heston stochastic-volatility model, which describes the pricing of European call options. A new neural network architecture, BeTINN, is proposed, extending time-induced modulation with multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a residual pathway, to improve accuracy and sensitivity predictions. Experiments using 15,000 interior points and 100,000 points for initial/boundary conditions demonstrate that BeTINN outperforms baseline methods in both normalized option value and sensitivity metrics, with further analysis revealing a disconnect between validation physics loss and derivative fidelity. The evaluation relies on a semi-analytic Heston oracle for reference values and sensitivities.

items.abstract: We study a spherical perfectly matched layer (PML) method for the time-harmonic Maxwell scattering problem with large wavenumber. Using vector spherical harmonics and a modal transformation for the coupled transverse magnetic components, we establish the sharp wavenumber-explicit stability estimate for the truncated PML problem and prove that its inf-sup constant is of order $O(κ^{-1})$. We then analyze the first-order Nédélec edge element method and its continuous interior penalty counterpart. Under the condition that $κ^3h^2$ is sufficiently small, the preasymptotic errors in the energy norm and the $κ$-scaled $\mathbf{L}^2$ norm are of orders $O(κh+κ^3h^2)$ and $O(κ^2h^2+κ^3h^2)$, respectively. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.

plain.summary: The work addresses the simulation of electromagnetic wave propagation using a specialized boundary condition technique to absorb outgoing waves. A mathematical framework involving vector spherical harmonics and finite element methods is developed to ensure the stability and accuracy of the numerical scheme, particularly when dealing with high-frequency phenomena. The analysis focuses on error estimates related to the discretization and the impact of the wavenumber on the solution’s precision, validated through computational experiments.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a spherical perfectly matched layer (PML) method to solve time-harmonic Maxwell scattering problems, specifically addressing challenges posed by large wave numbers. The method utilizes vector spherical harmonics and a modal transformation to analyze the truncated PML problem, deriving a wavenumber-explicit stability estimate and an inf-sup constant of order $O(κ^{-1})$. Numerical experiments employing Nédélec edge element and continuous interior penalty methods on tetrahedral meshes generated by Gmsh were conducted to validate the theoretical findings, revealing pollution errors and numerical reflections influenced by the PML profile.

items.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
items.abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

It reaches a minimum of $2.6\times 10^{-2}$ at the true value of $L=2.00\,\mathrm{mH}$ and quickly increases to the $\pm 8\%$ extremes. Capacitance sweep. Varying $C$ between $4.60$ – $5.40\,\upmu\mathrm{F}$ induces a stable, nearly parabolic trend in total RMSE. Throughout the range, the RMSE fluctuation is less than $5\times 10^{-3}$, demonstrating remarkable stability. This confirms that increasing precision leads to declining gains in prediction fidelity after $C$ is predicted within a few percent.

The total error for $r_{L}$ drops monotonically in the range of $0.460\!-\!0.540\,\Omega$, reaching a minimum at $r_{L}=0.52\,\Omega$. Overestimating significantly dampens the converter and improves the fit, whereas underestimating can inflate the RMSE by about 40%. Leakage resistance sweep. Changing $r_{C}$ between $27.6$ and $32.4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ leaves all traces essentially flat; a full $\pm 8\%$ perturbation moves the total RMSE by less than 1 %. The leakage path carries micro-ampere currents under normal load, because its exact value has negligible impact on one-step prediction. The suggested sequential-learning framework’s parameter release order is supported by the sensitivity data in Fig. 7. The monotonic fall in the series ESR and the prominent U-shape obtained when scanning the inductance illustrate that a tiny bias in either $L$ or $r_{L}$ directly generates a large voltage-channel RMSE. The capacitance curve is nearly flat, while the leakage-resistance trace is nearly horizontal. This suggests that moderate faults in $C$ or $r_{C}$ have minimal impact on one-step-ahead performance.

plain.summary: This work addresses the challenge of accurately determining component values within a power electronic circuit using limited data. A novel architecture, termed a staged PINN, is developed to sequentially learn the parameters, guided by a sensitivity analysis of the circuit’s behavior. The staged approach significantly improves the accuracy and speed of parameter estimation compared to a simultaneous training method, demonstrating robustness to component variations. The resulting model achieves high precision in identifying inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the problem of accurately estimating component values in a DC buck converter using limited time-domain data. A physics-informed neural network (PINN) is developed, employing a sequential training strategy where parameters are estimated in a specific order (inductance, capacitance, series ESR, and leakage resistance). The resulting model achieves an RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms, demonstrating improved performance compared to a simultaneous training approach, and exhibits robustness to component perturbations, as confirmed by an 84 factorial sweep.
